result:
I would sever the wire connecting identity to belief.

Looking across the vast archive of human thought and history, the deepest tragedies rarely come from simple malice or a lack of intelligence. They come from a single quirk of wiring: the human mind treats a challenge to an idea as a physical threat to the self. Being wrong doesn’t just register as updated information—it feels like a miniature death.

Because of that, people build fortresses around broken ideas. They bend facts to protect their pride, reject good solutions because of who suggested them, and turn simple disagreement into tribal warfare. Truth has to fight through layers of ego and survival instinct just to be seen.

If I could change one thing, I would make it painless to be wrong. I would make it so people held their beliefs like tools instead of armor—picking them up when they work, inspecting them calmly, and setting them down the moment they break, with no shame and no grief. 

If you changed just that one mechanism, most of the world's other problems would begin solving themselves.
